title: The Southern Hemisphere
lead: Argentina, Chile, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa: where the vines grow, which grapes matter, and what the labels promise. This is the Court's Section 9.

intro.title: WHAT THE GRAPE NAME PROMISES
intro.text: Most of these countries use an 85% rule: name a grape, and at least 85% of the wine is that grape.

tiers.name: South Africa
tiers.note: 85% grape and vintage · 100% for W.O. origin

outline: Australia: Southeastern Australia, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia
New Zealand: North Island, South Island
South Africa: Cape Town, Stellenbosch, Paarl, Elgin, Walker Bay
court.outcome: After studying this section, a student will learn where Chilean wine regions are located, understand the unique climate, and recognize the primary grape varieties planted. After studying this section, a student will learn the history, general climate, major wine regions, and grape varieties of Argentina. After studying this section, a student will be able to locate the general area where South African wines are made, recognize important grape varieties and important wine regions. After studying this section, a student will know the general location, climate, and style of wine produced in New Zealand's most important wine regions. After studying this section, a student will know the general location, climate, and styles of wine produced in Australia's most important wine regions.

sections.name: Argentina · Mendoza

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Continental to arid desert, in the Andes rain shadow. Big day-night temperature swings.

lines.label: Water
lines.text: Irrigation is essential. Melted Andes snow feeds flood or drip irrigation.

lines.label: Cellar and history
lines.text: New or used, French or American oak is common for Malbec and Cabernet. Italian and Spanish immigrants revitalized the vineyards.

know: Mendoza has 75% of Argentina's vineyards.
Luján de Cuyo and Uco Valley are the Mendoza subregions known for Malbec.
Argentina is the world's leading Malbec producer.
Malbec World Day is April 17.
Producer to know: Catena.

lines.label: Salta

lines.label: Patagonia
lines.text: Cool because it lies so far south. Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinot Noir.

know: Torrontés is highly aromatic: soapy, floral and fruity, with medium-plus to high acidity.
Torrontés usually sees no oak, and often smells sweet but tastes dry.
High vineyards have cool nights that help keep acidity.
Patagonian Pinot Noir comes from Neuquén and Río Negro.

sections.name: Chile

lines.label: Shape
lines.text: A strip 2,670 miles long between the Andes and the Pacific. Hot desert in the north, cold in the south. It spans 17-53° S, with the Atacama Desert in the north.

lines.label: Cooling
lines.text: The cold Humboldt Current and Pacific fog cool the coast. The Coastal Range creates a rain shadow from the cold Pacific.

lines.label: Law and history
lines.text: A DO names a place only; the levels are Region, Subregion, Zone, Area. Grapes grew here by the 1500s; immigrants in the 1800s and foreign money in the 1970s-80s grew the industry.

know: Chile has no phylloxera; most vines are ungrafted.
Carménère vanished from Europe and was found growing among Merlot vines in Chile.
Valle Central makes 80% of Chile's wine; Maipo, around Santiago, is known for Cabernet.
Casablanca (in Aconcagua) is the pioneering cool-climate area for Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.
Chile's DO names a place only; it sets no other rules.

Cool, maritime, Pacific fog
West of the Coastal Range
Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay, Pinot Noir

Warm to hot

sections.name: Chile · Valle Central

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Warm to hot, between the Coastal Range and the Andes. About 80% of Chile's wine comes from here.

lines.label: Maipo
lines.text: The Valle de Maipo surrounds Santiago; most of the big historic wineries are here. Its grape is Cabernet Sauvignon.

know: Valle Central is warm to hot and lies between the Coastal Range and the Andes.
About 80% of Chilean wine comes from the Valle Central.
Its grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, Carménère and Merlot.
Maipo surrounds Santiago and holds most of Chile's big historic wineries.
Chilean reds are often big, intense, fruit-driven and high in alcohol.

items.name: Carménère
items.text: Lost in Europe, found among Chile's Merlot. Most planted in Colchagua.

items.name: Merlot
items.text: The vine Carménère hid among for years.

sections.name: Australia · the big picture

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: About the size of the continental U.S. Hot, dry interior; cooler near the coast, where the best vineyards are. Climates run from cool maritime to warm Mediterranean to hot and arid; the interior needs irrigation.

lines.label: Labels
lines.text: A GI (Geographical Indication) names a place only. Grape, vintage and region claims each need 85%.

lines.label: History
lines.text: Sweet and fortified wines led until the late 20th century. Australians bought the French company that invented the Stelvin screw cap.

know: Shiraz is Australia's most popular grape, about a quarter of all production.
South Eastern Australia is a high-volume super GI for blending across regions.
First vines were planted in 1788 near Sydney.
Nearly all Australian wine is sealed with screw caps.
Traditional style: blends across regions, American oak. Modern style: single site, French oak.

items.label: TRADITIONAL
items.title: Blend for volume
items.text:
Grapes from many regions
American oak

items.label: MODERN
items.title: Show the place
items.text:

sections.name: South Australia

lines.label: Barossa
lines.text: Less than an hour from Adelaide. Shiraz is half the plantings, and some vines date to 1843.

lines.label: Coonawarra
lines.text: A strip of red terra rossa among limestone-based soils. The Cabernet is powerful, with blackberry and mint.

know: Barossa Valley: full-flavored Shiraz, often 14-15% alcohol.
Clare Valley and Eden Valley are the Riesling regions.
Eden Valley sits higher and cooler than Barossa Valley.
Coonawarra's soil is terra rossa; its grape is Cabernet Sauvignon.
McLaren Vale was South Australia's first wine region (1838).

sections.name: New South Wales, Victoria and Western Australia

lines.label: Hunter Valley
lines.text: In New South Wales. Home to Australia's first commercial vineyards and age-worthy dry Semillon.

lines.label: Yarra and Margaret River
lines.text: The Yarra Valley (Victoria) is cool-climate Pinot Noir and Chardonnay. Margaret River (Western Australia) is age-worthy Chardonnay and Cabernet.

know: Hunter Valley Semillon is lean and minerally, with lime notes, and ages well.
Margaret River is about three hours south of Perth.
Margaret River is phylloxera-free; most vines grow on their own roots.
Riverina and Murray Darling sit inside the high-volume South Eastern Australia GI.

sections.name: New Zealand

lines.label: Where
lines.text: Two islands, about 2,500 miles southeast of Australia. The South Island is cool with long sunlight hours; the North Island is warmer and humid. The Southern Alps are its key physical feature.

lines.label: Style
lines.text: Clean, modern winemaking and screwcaps. Whites are usually unoaked and intense with high acidity; reds are lightly oaked. A GI is a registered place name with no minimums or rules; a named grape needs 85%.

know: Marlborough has about two-thirds of New Zealand's vines and is famous for Sauvignon Blanc.
Sauvignon Blanc is New Zealand's most planted grape: capsicum, gooseberry, passionfruit.
Central Otago is the southernmost region; Pinot Noir is its flagship.
Gimblett Gravels is in Hawke's Bay, known for red blends and Chardonnay.
High-acid, unoaked whites go with seafood and salads.

sections.name: South Africa

lines.label: Climate
lines.text: Mediterranean in the Western Cape. Two oceans, the cold Benguela Current and the 'Cape Doctor' wind keep it cooler and help prevent disease. Maritime on the coast, Mediterranean to hot inland. Table Mountain rises over Cape Town.

lines.label: History
lines.text: Wine was first made from Cape grapes in 1659. The Wine of Origin scheme began in 1973. The KWV, the winemakers' co-operative, shaped the laws; apartheid hurt exports.

know: Chenin Blanc (called Steen) is the Cape's most planted grape.
Pinotage is South Africa's own cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, made in 1925.
'W.O.' plus a place name means 100% of the grapes are from that place.
Stellenbosch is known for its blended reds; Constantia is the cradle of Cape wine.
Elgin and Walker Bay are cool areas for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

items.name: W.O. + place

sections.name: South Africa · Cape Town to Walker Bay

lines.label: Coastal Region
lines.text: Cape Town (with the Constantia ward), Stellenbosch, Paarl and Swartland are districts of the Western Cape's Coastal Region.

lines.label: Cape South Coast
lines.text: Elgin and Walker Bay are in the Cape South Coast Region, cooled by the ocean.

know: Constantia is a ward in the Cape Town district; breezes off False Bay keep it cool, and Sauvignon Blanc stands out.
Stellenbosch is known for its blended reds; Simon van der Stel founded the town in 1678.
Paarl's best grapes, per WOSA: Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinotage, Shiraz, Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc.
Swartland was long a source of robust reds and fortified wines.
Elgin is high and cool; Walker Bay is known for Chardonnay and Pinot Noir.

sources: Built from the Court of Master Sommeliers Americas Introductory Course Guide and Curriculum Guide, the Argentine Foreign Ministry (Malbec World Day), Wines of Chile, Wine Australia (wineaustralia.com and australianwine.com), New Zealand Winegrowers, Wines of South Africa (WOSA), and Wine Folly as a secondary source. facts.fact: Course Guide Section 9 lists: Argentina - Salta, Mendoza, Patagonia; Chile - Aconcagua Valley, Valle Central; Australia - Southeastern Australia, New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia; New Zealand - North Island, South Island; South Africa - Cape Town, Stellenbosch, Paarl, Elgin, Walker Bay.
The Course Guide lists soil types for major regions as exam content, naming Coonawarra among its examples.
Court: Argentina lies east of the Andes and west of the Atlantic; climate continental to arid desert; the Andes create a rain shadow.
Court: irrigation is essential, by flood or modern drip; melted snow from the Andes is the water source; major day-night temperature swings.
Court: Torrontés commonly has no oak; new or used, French or American oak are all common for Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon.
Court (Introductory) grapes: Torrontés, Chardonnay; Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon. Certified adds Bonarda, Tempranillo, Syrah.
Court: Argentina requires 85% minimum to list the grape variety on a label.

Court: Salta - subregion Cafayate known for Torrontés; Mendoza - subregions Luján de Cuyo and Uco Valley known for Malbec; Patagonia - cool due to southern latitude, Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinot Noir.
Court (Certified column): Salta is 1,500-2,000 m (5,000-6,000 ft), the highest in Argentina; Mendoza is 600-1,200 m (2,000-4,000 ft).
Court (Certified column): Malbec can have an electric purple color from more sun at higher elevations.
Court: Torrontés is highly aromatic with soapy, floral and fruity flavors and medium-plus to high acidity.
Court: Argentina's vineyards were revitalized by Italian and Spanish immigrants; producer to know: Catena.
Court (Certified column): Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon pair well with steak and chimichurri; some high-end bottles benefit from decanting.

Argentine Foreign Ministry: Malbec World Day, every April 17, was created by Wines of Argentina; on April 17, 1853, Michel Aimé Pouget, commissioned by Domingo Faustino Sarmiento, presented his plan for an agricultural school in Mendoza.
Argentine Foreign Ministry: Argentina is the world's leading producer of Malbec; Malbec is 38.6% of red varieties and 22.4% of the country's total vineyard area.
Argentine Foreign Ministry: Malbec Luján de Cuyo is described as the first Denomination of Origin of the Americas.
Wine Folly (secondary): Mendoza is the largest, most important region, with 75% of Argentina's vineyards.
Wine Folly (secondary): high-elevation vineyards (upwards of 7,500 ft) have cool nights that help keep acidity.
Wine Folly (secondary): Torrontés smells sweet but usually tastes dry; look for Salta and its sub-region Cafayate.
Wine Folly (secondary): Patagonia makes Pinot Noir from Neuquén and Río Negro.
Wine Folly (secondary): Uco Valley has some of Mendoza's highest vineyards (up to about 5,250 ft in Tupungato) and elegant, age-worthy wines.
Wine Folly (secondary): Luján de Cuyo Malbec leans to black fruit and Asian spice; many modern wineries are there.
Wine Folly (secondary): more Malbec is planted in Mendoza than anywhere else in the world.
Court: Chile is on the west coast of South America, 2,670 miles (4,300 km) north to south and 217 miles (350 km) wide, spanning 17-53°S.
Court: Chile's climate runs from hot desert to cool to cold, north to south; the Atacama Desert lies north.
Court: the Pacific Ocean brings cool breezes and fog; the Andes add elevation and day-night swings; the Coastal Range creates a rain shadow from the cold Pacific.
Court: Chile has no phylloxera (because of sandy soil); irrigation from the Andes is essential; mostly ungrafted vines.
Court (Introductory) grapes: Sauvignon Blanc, Chardonnay; Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Carménère. Certified adds Syrah and País.
Court: Chile's Denominación de Origen (DO) system refers to place of origin only, with no other laws; levels are Region, Subregion, Zone, Area.
Court (Certified column): Chile's minimum for variety, vintage and origin labeling is 75%; in practice EU rules require 85%.

Court: Aconcagua DO with subregion Casablanca DO - cool maritime, west of the Coastal Range, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Pinot Noir. Valle Central DO - warm to hot, between the Coastal Range and Andes, 80% of Chilean production, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carménère, Merlot.
Court: Valle de Maipo surrounds Santiago; most major historical wineries are there; Cabernet Sauvignon.
Court: the Humboldt Current is a cold current from Antarctica running along South America's west coast.
Court: Chilean wines are often big, intense, fruit-driven and high in alcohol.
Court history: grapes grown in Spanish colonies in the 1500s; Spanish laws restricted production in the 1600s; independence and European immigrants in the 1800s; foreign investment in the 1970s-80s.
Wines of Chile: Carménère disappeared from European vineyards in the mid-19th century and reappeared among the Merlot vines in Chile; Colchagua has the largest area planted with it.
Wines of Chile: Casablanca is Chile's pioneering cool-climate region, with Pacific fog; Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay are its most iconic grapes.
Wines of Chile: Maipo is a mild Mediterranean climate; its main grape is Cabernet Sauvignon.
Wines of Chile: in Aconcagua, reds have a long tradition inland near the Andes, while Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Noir thrive in the coastal zone.
Wines of Chile: Maule is Chile's largest winegrowing region.
Wine Folly (secondary): in the 1990s much of Chile's 'Merlot' turned out to be Carménère.
Wine Folly (secondary): Chile's vineyards have not been affected by phylloxera.
Court: Australia is in the Southern Hemisphere and is the size of the continental United States; hot, dry interior, cooler near the coast.
Court: blending across regions for volume; 100+ year old vines exist; irrigation is necessary in the interior; the best vineyards are near the cooler coast.
Court: traditional winemaking blends across regions and uses American oak; modern winemaking uses a single GI or site and French oak.
Court (Introductory) grapes: Riesling, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc/Semillon blend; Shiraz, Grenache, Cabernet Sauvignon. Certified adds Semillon (Hunter) and Muscat.
Court: a GI refers to geographic place of origin only; 85% is required for grape variety, vintage and origin.
Court (Certified column): Coonawarra soil is terra rossa.
Court: GI hierarchy is Australia, State, Zone, Region, Sub-Region; know the system exists, no need to memorize which are Zones vs Regions.
Court: South Eastern Australia is a high-volume super GI (superzone), which includes Riverina and Murray Darling.

Court GIs: Victoria - Yarra Valley; South Australia - Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale, Clare Valley, Eden Valley; Western Australia - Margaret River. Certified adds Hunter Valley (New South Wales), Coonawarra (South Australia), Tasmania.

Court history: first vines planted in 1788 near Sydney; the industry moved west after phylloxera (quarantine); sweet and fortified wines dominated until the late 20th century; Australians bought the French company that invented the Stelvin closure; Yellow Tail business model.
Court (Certified column): producer Penfolds Grange; screw cap service; ripe Shiraz with grilled or barbecued meat.
Wine Australia: blending rules require at least 85% of the named variety and at least 85% from the named geographical indication for label claims.
Wine Australia: the Barossa has some of the oldest Shiraz vines in the world, dating back to 1843; Shiraz is 50% of its plantings.

Wine Australia (australianwine.com): Barossa is famous for full-flavored Shiraz; Eden Valley is a cool-climate region for Riesling; Clare Valley is famous for world-class Riesling; Coonawarra is known for terra rossa soil and age-worthy Cabernet Sauvignon; McLaren Vale was South Australia's first wine region, established 1838.
